content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Other hand-carried suction devices give the user a reading or a signal of some kind. A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the handle structure carrying a battery and a vacuum electric pump connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, together with an air pressure sensor, a display screen, a switch button, a pressure relief valve, and a USB charging port, the display screen displaying the negative pressure value of the suction cup and the battery power [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. What that device offers the operator is a number to be read: negative pressure is monitored and displayed in real time, and the reference does not describe a level at which the device itself declares that the grip is going. A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has likewise been described in which a vacuum pump is arranged on a suction cup body having a handle fixed at its upper end, a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, and the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge, with a light source that displays different usage states, and with a buzzer that sends out alarm sounds according to different usage states, air being pumped out continuously so as to avoid loosening and falling during movement [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. There again the answer to a decaying grip is to keep pumping, and the alarm follows a usage state rather than any stated relationship to the vacuum at which the cup would let the load go.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has also been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle, at least one electrical vacuum pump, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume between a cup and an attachment surface, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally with a power storage unit and with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The indicator described there reports that attachment has been achieved, that is, it responds to a vacuum level lying above a threshold; the threshold that governs a falling vacuum in that device is the minimum vacuum level at which the pump is run again.
14	
15	Cordless hand tools that grip by suction are themselves long established. A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip whose perimeter region is contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light emitting diodes of different colours that indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected to the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. That indication is drawn from the state of the power source rather than from a measurement of the vacuum that is holding the object. In a sucker for plate glass, a sucker body carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel by way of a piston lever that moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The vacuum in that device is raised by hand, and the predetermined value at which the sound generator is turned on is the point at which the piston lever closes the switch; the reference does not relate that value to the vacuum below which the sucker would cease to retain the sheet it is carrying.
16	
17	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
18	
19	Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip such as battery state, on the achievement of attachment, on a rate of change, as a displayed number that the operator must read and interpret while carrying a slab, or at a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
20	
21	Third, much of the equipment that does monitor vacuum carefully is not something a person can carry. It sits on a frame, a boom, or a mounting frame, and it depends on a hose to a remote vacuum source, a mains or vehicle supply, a reservoir, or a controller and interface that are not part of the tool. On such equipment the decision about a failing grip can be taken away from the operator and acted on by the machine. A tool that is taken up a ladder or onto a scaffold in one hand has no machine to act for it, and the only person who can act on a failing grip is the one holding it.
22	
23	There remains a need for a cordless hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip vacuum is being lost while the suction cup is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped.
24

I have read all sources and draft files. Building the ledger now.

**Source authority (USER passages only):** the disclosure paragraph + 2 claims + numbered paragraph in `input/disclosure.md`, repeated verbatim as the first USER turn in `input/conversation.md`; plus two corrective USER turns (remove "QA MARKER ONE" from the Field; reword the Background opening). That authorizes: cordless handheld vacuum lifter; rigid body 14 with handle 16; suction cup 10 carried by rigid body, carrying flexible sealing lip 12; electric vacuum pump 20 inside the rigid body drawing air **through a port 22 to create a vacuum**; pressure sensor 30 monitoring the grip vacuum; warning indicator 32 driven by the sensor, activating when vacuum is lost and before a load can be dropped; rechargeable battery 40 powering the pump; use "for glass and stone panels".

Everything else in the draft I traced item by item; the gaps are below.

input.summary:
The draft's core apparatus skeleton (rigid body 14 / handle 16 / suction cup 10 / flexible sealing lip 12 / electric vacuum pump 20 / port 22 / pressure sensor 30 / warning indicator 32 / rechargeable battery 40, and the "activate when vacuum is lost, before a load can be dropped" relationship) traces cleanly to the single USER disclosure passage, which is repeated verbatim as the first USER turn of the conversation. The two later USER turns are corrective only (remove "QA MARKER ONE" from the Field; begin the Background with "A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to"); both are honored in draft/04-field.md and draft/05-background.md, and neither adds technical matter. Title, "Not applicable." cross-reference, and "Not applicable." government-support statement match input/brief.md. No drafting notes, placeholders, or open questions survive in any draft section, the section line 2-2 designation is repeated consistently across the FIG. 1 brief, the FIG. 2 brief, draft/07-drawings.md and the detailed description, and the numeral table is internally consistent with the per-figure numeral lists.

The ledger is not clean, however. The largest gap is an entire structural concept that the inventor never states: the "sealed region 18". The disclosure says only that the pump is "configured to draw air through a port to create a vacuum" and says nothing about a space between the cup and the workpiece, about the sealing lip bounding anything, or about where the port opens. The draft nevertheless makes the sealed region a numbered part, a claim 1 limitation ("configured to bound a sealed region between the suction cup and a workpiece"), a method-claim limitation, a defined term, and a cross-hatching-and-contact-topology instruction in the FIG. 2 brief ("bounded above by the underside of the suction cup 10, at its edge by the flexible sealing lip 12, and below by the upper face of the workpiece 50"), together with the flow-boundary statement "The port 22 opens out of the sealed region 18." Notably, "sealing units that bound a sealed space" is the very structure the Background attributes to US-10625955-B2, so this is imported prior-art structure rather than inventor structure, and the port/boundary statements are expressly substantive under the functional-surface rule.

Beyond that, ten further categories of untraced matter appear: (a) the location of the warning indicator 32 "on the rigid body 14"; (b) the FIG. 4 trace profile — rise, "levels off for a short interval", then decay "without rising again" — and the placement of the activation mark to the right of that plateau; (c) the panel-handling assertions in the detailed description (panels "heavy", "carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension", "break when dropped"); (d) the clamping/deflection mechanism (lip "deflects and conforms", atmosphere "clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14", "clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum" in claims 3 and 6); (e) the enumerated leak causes (dust or grit under the lip, textured or porous face, damaged lip, flexing of the workpiece); (f) the comparative advantage argument carried out of the Background into the Summary and detailed description (frame-mounted lifters with a second vacuum source, a reservoir, or a motion interlock; pump-restart devices); (g) the set-down scenarios (stand, wall, stack); (h) the FIG. 1 staging — near-horizontal panel "as when a panel is lifted from a stack", suction cup below the body, handle with "open space beneath it for the user's fingers" — which also contradicts the near-vertical attitude asserted in the description; (i) the comparing-step 208 decision-and-loop control logic in FIG. 5 and the description; and (j) the FIG. 1 instruction that leads both 100 and 14 to the same plain enclosure.

Two verified internal inconsistencies are independent of source support: numeral 32 is used both for the physical warning indicator and, in the FIG. 4 brief, for an event point on the trace ("Lead the numeral 32 to that mark"), so the numeral means two things; and the FIG. 2 caption in draft/07-drawings.md places "the sealed region ... within the rigid body", which contradicts the same draft's own topology in which the sealed region lies between the cup, the lip and the workpiece face. One formalities defect remains in the Summary: "and that is what the user spends in getting the panel onto a stand" has no antecedent for "that" — a dangling remnant of a removed "warning interval" concept (the conversation records an earlier draft in which FIG. 4 "dimensions the resulting warning interval").

I did not assess patentability, novelty, or the accuracy of the prior-art characterizations in the Background, and I did not inspect any rendered image. Sixteen findings follow, each with the candidate wording, the nearest source passage showing the gap, and a filing-clean fix.

findings.title: "Sealed region 18" is an undisclosed numbered part and an undisclosed claim limitation
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claims 1 and 4; draft/06-summary.md ¶3, ¶11; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3, ¶7, ¶9, ¶19, ¶31; draft/10-abstract.md; draft/numerals.md line 9; figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-LIFTER.md
findings.detail: The draft introduces a sealed region as a numbered part, makes the sealing lip's bounding of it a positive limitation of independent claims 1 and 4, and gives it an explicit contact topology in the FIG. 2 brief. No USER passage mentions a sealed region, a space between the cup and the workpiece, or any bounding function for the sealing lip. The inventor's pump limitation is unqualified as to where the air comes from. The draft's own Background attributes "first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space" to US-10625955-B2, so this structure is imported from prior art, not from the inventor. Under the functional-surface rule, the bounding statement is substantive contact topology and a flow boundary, not a depiction convention.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 1: "a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip configured to bound a sealed region between the suction cup and a workpiece when the flexible sealing lip is placed against the workpiece" and "configured to draw air from the sealed region through a port to establish a grip vacuum in the sealed region". Candidate, FIG. 2 brief: "The sealed region 18 is the enclosed space bounded above by the underside of the suction cup 10, at its edge by the flexible sealing lip 12, and below by the upper face of the workpiece 50. That space is left clear of hatching." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 12, identical at input/conversation.md line 14): "an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body, the electric vacuum pump configured to draw air through a port to create a vacuum". No affirmative passage in the disclosure or in any USER turn recites a sealed region or a bounding function.
findings.fix: Delete numeral 18 and every recitation of the sealed region. In claim 1 restore "a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip;" and "an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body, the electric vacuum pump configured to draw air through a port to create a grip vacuum, the grip vacuum retaining a load on the suction cup;". In claim 4 replace the placing step with "placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece;" and the evacuating step with "drawing air through a port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery, so as to create a grip vacuum;". In draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3 define the term without the region: "The grip vacuum is the vacuum created by the electric vacuum pump 20 and monitored by the pressure sensor 30, expressed as a positive magnitude. The grip vacuum rises as air is removed by the electric vacuum pump 20 and falls as air leaks back. The grip vacuum is lost when air leaks back and the grip vacuum falls." Make the corresponding deletions in ¶7, ¶9, ¶19 and ¶31, in draft/06-summary.md ¶3 and ¶11, and in draft/10-abstract.md ("a suction cup carrying a flexible sealing lip"). Remove the sealed-region bullet and the numeral 18 rows/lists from the FIG. 2 brief.

findings.title: Port 22 is given an undisclosed flow-boundary location
findings.detail: The draft states where the port opens. Port location relative to a flow boundary is expressly substantive even in a schematic figure. The inventor discloses only that the pump draws air through a port; nothing states that the port opens out of any region, chamber, or face.
findings.evidence: Candidate, description ¶9: "The port 22 opens out of the sealed region 18." Candidate, FIG. 2 brief: "The port 22 is an aperture opening out of the sealed region 18." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 19): "An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum." No source passage locates the port.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence "The port 22 opens out of the sealed region 18." from ¶9. In the FIG. 2 brief replace the bullet with "The port 22 is an aperture through which the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air; lead the numeral 22 to that aperture." Amend the FIG. 2 caption in draft/07-drawings.md to "...showing the electric vacuum pump and the port."

findings.title: Warning indicator 32 is placed on the rigid body without source support
findings.detail: The application text, not merely the figure brief, asserts a mounting location for the warning indicator. The disclosure says only that the sensor drives the indicator; it never says where the indicator is, nor that it is carried on the body, and the drafting agent's own conversation turn records the indicator modality and placement as an open gap it did not fill.
findings.evidence: Candidate, description ¶5: "A warning indicator 32 is on the rigid body 14." Candidate, FIG. 1 brief: "The warning indicator 32 is shown schematically as a small discrete element on the rigid body 14." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 19): "The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost." No source passage locates the indicator.
findings.fix: Delete "A warning indicator 32 is on the rigid body 14." from ¶5. Remove numeral 32 from the FIG. 1 brief, from its two numeral lists, and from the FIG. 1 depiction bullets; the warning indicator remains shown in the FIG. 3 schematic, where no location is asserted.

findings.title: FIG. 4 trace profile asserts an undisclosed working-vacuum plateau and monotonic decay
findings.detail: The brief prescribes a specific operating history: a rise, a plateau of stated duration, then a decay that never rises again, with the activation mark placed to the right of the plateau. The plateau asserts a sustained working vacuum and the never-rising decay asserts that the pump does not restore the vacuum after the leak begins. Both are operating conditions with technical substance, and both are the drafting agent's argument rather than inventor matter. No USER passage describes any vacuum-versus-time behavior.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The grip vacuum trace 60 is a solid curve that rises from the origin, levels off for a short interval, and then decays, falling smoothly and without rising again, continuing downwards towards the right of the drawing area." and "A small open circle marks a point on the decaying part of the grip vacuum trace 60, above the time axis 72 and to the right of the levelled-off part of the trace." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 19): "The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before a load can be dropped." No source passage describes a plateau, a decay shape, or a time axis.
findings.fix: Replace the two bullets with: "The grip vacuum trace 60 is a solid curve that rises from the origin and then falls, showing a grip vacuum that is established and is subsequently lost." and "A small open circle marks a point on the falling part of the grip vacuum trace 60, above the time axis 72. That mark is the point at which the warning indicator activates."

findings.title: Undisclosed panel-handling assertions: weight, near-vertical attitude, shear and tension loading, breakage
findings.detail: The paragraph asserts how glass and stone panels are carried and how the grip is loaded. Attitude of carriage and the decomposition of the grip load into shear and tension are technical substance about operating conditions. The disclosure's only statement about panels is the field of use.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "such panels are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 19): "A cordless handheld vacuum lifter for glass and stone panels is disclosed." No source passage addresses panel weight, carrying attitude, load direction, or breakage.
findings.fix: Delete the quoted clause and end the paragraph after "...for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended."

findings.title: Undisclosed clamping and lip-deflection mechanism recited in the description and in claims 3 and 6
findings.detail: The draft recites that the lip deflects and conforms to the face, that atmospheric pressure clamps the cup and with it the rigid body to the workpiece, and, in dependent claims, that the lip conforms and seals "under a clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum". These are contact-topology and force-path statements. The inventor discloses a flexible sealing lip and a vacuum, and no mechanism, deflection, conformance, or clamping relationship. Common engineering knowledge is not inventor support.
findings.evidence: Candidate, ¶7: "When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to the face of the workpiece 50". Candidate, ¶9: "the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14, to the workpiece 50". Candidate, claim 6: "the flexible sealing lip conforms to a face of the panel under a clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum". Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 11): "a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip". No source passage describes deflection, conformance, or clamping.
findings.fix: In ¶7 keep only "The suction cup 10 comprises the flexible sealing lip 12, which is placed against the workpiece 50." In ¶9 delete the clause beginning "the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere" and end the sentence at "...and so raises the grip vacuum, so that the grip vacuum retains a load on the suction cup 10." Amend claim 3 to "wherein the workpiece is a glass or stone panel." and claim 6 to "wherein the workpiece is a glass or stone panel." In ¶29 and in draft/06-summary.md ¶3 delete the corresponding conform/clamp clauses.

findings.title: Undisclosed enumerated leak causes in the detailed description
findings.detail: The description lists specific seal-failure mechanisms as operating conditions of the invention. These appear in the Background as prior-art context, but prior art cannot support invention text, and no USER passage names any leak cause.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds into the sealed region 18 and the grip vacuum trace 60 falls." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 19): "The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost." No source passage identifies any cause of vacuum loss.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "If the grip vacuum is lost, the grip vacuum trace 60 falls."

findings.title: Comparative advantage argument about other equipment carried into the Summary and detailed description
findings.detail: Outside the Background, the draft asserts what frame-mounted, suspended and pump-restart devices do — a second vacuum source, a reservoir, a motion interlock, running the pump instead of warning — and builds the advantage of the invention on those assertions. The Background exemption for prior-art characterizations does not reach the Summary or the detailed description, and no USER passage makes any comparison to other equipment. The conversation records these three paragraphs as the drafting agent's own argument.
findings.evidence: Candidate, ¶27: "Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip, such as a second vacuum source, a reservoir, or an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these". Candidate, ¶25: "This is a different design decision from answering a falling grip vacuum by running a pump again." Candidate, summary ¶9: "A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 17): "The cordless handheld vacuum lifter of claim 1, wherein the warning indicator is configured to activate before a load can be dropped." The only inventor statement of purpose is the warning timing itself.
findings.fix: Delete draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶25 and ¶27 in full and draft/06-summary.md ¶9 in full. The supported statement of purpose already stands in summary ¶7 and description ¶23 once those paragraphs are corrected per the next finding.

findings.title: Undisclosed set-down scenarios and user actions
findings.detail: The draft states what the user does with the warning: walking the panel to a stand, setting it against a wall, lowering it onto the stack, and setting the workpiece down as a method step. No USER passage describes any user action after the warning; the disclosure states only that the indicator warns before a load can be dropped.
findings.evidence: Candidate, ¶23: "The user is told while the load is still held, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast". Candidate, ¶33: "...and the user sets the workpiece 50 down." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 19): "The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before a load can be dropped."
findings.fix: Replace ¶23 with: "The warning indicator 32 is activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped." In ¶33 end the sentence at "...before the load can be dropped." In draft/06-summary.md ¶7 keep only "The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum is lost, while the suction cup is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped." In draft/10-abstract.md end the last sentence at "...so that the user is warned before the load can be dropped."

findings.title: FIG. 1 staging asserts undisclosed panel attitude, use scenario, and handle finger clearance
findings.detail: The brief fixes the panel in a near-horizontal attitude taken from a stack, places the suction cup below the body, and gives the handle open space beneath it for the user's fingers. Relative location of the gripped panel, the use scenario, and finger clearance under the handle are technical substance, not a generic outline choice. The disclosure gives no attitude, no use scenario, and no handle geometry.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "...gripping the upper face of a workpiece 50 that lies in a near-horizontal attitude, as when a panel is lifted from a stack."; "The handle 16 is on the rigid body 14, with open space beneath it for the user's fingers."; "The suction cup 10 is on the rigid body 14, below it". Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 19): "The lifter includes a suction cup 10 that carries a flexible sealing lip 12 on a rigid body 14. The rigid body 14 also includes a handle 16." No source passage states an attitude, a stack, or any handle geometry.
findings.fix: Replace the "What is shown" line with "The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 with the flexible sealing lip 12 in contact with a face of a workpiece 50." Replace the handle bullet with "The handle 16 is on the rigid body 14; lead the numeral 16 to it." Replace the suction cup bullet with "The suction cup 10 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is shown schematically as a plain dish outline."

findings.title: Undisclosed decision-and-loop control logic in FIG. 5 and the method description
findings.detail: The draft adds a comparing step 208 implemented as a decision with a feedback branch that returns to the monitoring step. That is an iterative control algorithm with technical substance. The disclosure recites monitoring and activation only; the drafting agent's own turn records "threshold implementation" as a gap it did not fill.

structured_output.summary:
The draft's core apparatus skeleton (rigid body 14 / handle 16 / suction cup 10 / flexible sealing lip 12 / electric vacuum pump 20 / port 22 / pressure sensor 30 / warning indicator 32 / rechargeable battery 40, and the "activate when vacuum is lost, before a load can be dropped" relationship) traces cleanly to the single USER disclosure passage, which is repeated verbatim as the first USER turn of the conversation. The two later USER turns are corrective only (remove "QA MARKER ONE" from the Field; begin the Background with "A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to"); both are honored in draft/04-field.md and draft/05-background.md, and neither adds technical matter. Title, "Not applicable." cross-reference, and "Not applicable." government-support statement match input/brief.md. No drafting notes, placeholders, or open questions survive in any draft section, the section line 2-2 designation is repeated consistently across the FIG. 1 brief, the FIG. 2 brief, draft/07-drawings.md and the detailed description, and the numeral table is internally consistent with the per-figure numeral lists.

The ledger is not clean, however. The largest gap is an entire structural concept that the inventor never states: the "sealed region 18". The disclosure says only that the pump is "configured to draw air through a port to create a vacuum" and says nothing about a space between the cup and the workpiece, about the sealing lip bounding anything, or about where the port opens. The draft nevertheless makes the sealed region a numbered part, a claim 1 limitation ("configured to bound a sealed region between the suction cup and a workpiece"), a method-claim limitation, a defined term, and a cross-hatching-and-contact-topology instruction in the FIG. 2 brief ("bounded above by the underside of the suction cup 10, at its edge by the flexible sealing lip 12, and below by the upper face of the workpiece 50"), together with the flow-boundary statement "The port 22 opens out of the sealed region 18." Notably, "sealing units that bound a sealed space" is the very structure the Background attributes to US-10625955-B2, so this is imported prior-art structure rather than inventor structure, and the port/boundary statements are expressly substantive under the functional-surface rule.

Beyond that, ten further categories of untraced matter appear: (a) the location of the warning indicator 32 "on the rigid body 14"; (b) the FIG. 4 trace profile — rise, "levels off for a short interval", then decay "without rising again" — and the placement of the activation mark to the right of that plateau; (c) the panel-handling assertions in the detailed description (panels "heavy", "carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension", "break when dropped"); (d) the clamping/deflection mechanism (lip "deflects and conforms", atmosphere "clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14", "clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum" in claims 3 and 6); (e) the enumerated leak causes (dust or grit under the lip, textured or porous face, damaged lip, flexing of the workpiece); (f) the comparative advantage argument carried out of the Background into the Summary and detailed description (frame-mounted lifters with a second vacuum source, a reservoir, or a motion interlock; pump-restart devices); (g) the set-down scenarios (stand, wall, stack); (h) the FIG. 1 staging — near-horizontal panel "as when a panel is lifted from a stack", suction cup below the body, handle with "open space beneath it for the user's fingers" — which also contradicts the near-vertical attitude asserted in the description; (i) the comparing-step 208 decision-and-loop control logic in FIG. 5 and the description; and (j) the FIG. 1 instruction that leads both 100 and 14 to the same plain enclosure.

Two verified internal inconsistencies are independent of source support: numeral 32 is used both for the physical warning indicator and, in the FIG. 4 brief, for an event point on the trace ("Lead the numeral 32 to that mark"), so the numeral means two things; and the FIG. 2 caption in draft/07-drawings.md places "the sealed region ... within the rigid body", which contradicts the same draft's own topology in which the sealed region lies between the cup, the lip and the workpiece face. One formalities defect remains in the Summary: "and that is what the user spends in getting the panel onto a stand" has no antecedent for "that" — a dangling remnant of a removed "warning interval" concept (the conversation records an earlier draft in which FIG. 4 "dimensions the resulting warning interval").

I did not assess patentability, novelty, or the accuracy of the prior-art characterizations in the Background, and I did not inspect any rendered image. Sixteen findings follow, each with the candidate wording, the nearest source passage showing the gap, and a filing-clean fix.

findings.title: "Sealed region 18" is an undisclosed numbered part and an undisclosed claim limitation
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claims 1 and 4; draft/06-summary.md ¶3, ¶11; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3, ¶7, ¶9, ¶19, ¶31; draft/10-abstract.md; draft/numerals.md line 9; figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-LIFTER.md
findings.detail: The draft introduces a sealed region as a numbered part, makes the sealing lip's bounding of it a positive limitation of independent claims 1 and 4, and gives it an explicit contact topology in the FIG. 2 brief. No USER passage mentions a sealed region, a space between the cup and the workpiece, or any bounding function for the sealing lip. The inventor's pump limitation is unqualified as to where the air comes from. The draft's own Background attributes "first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space" to US-10625955-B2, so this structure is imported from prior art, not from the inventor. Under the functional-surface rule, the bounding statement is substantive contact topology and a flow boundary, not a depiction convention.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 1: "a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip configured to bound a sealed region between the suction cup and a workpiece when the flexible sealing lip is placed against the workpiece" and "configured to draw air from the sealed region through a port to establish a grip vacuum in the sealed region". Candidate, FIG. 2 brief: "The sealed region 18 is the enclosed space bounded above by the underside of the suction cup 10, at its edge by the flexible sealing lip 12, and below by the upper face of the workpiece 50. That space is left clear of hatching." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md line 12, identical at input/conversation.md line 14): "an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body, the electric vacuum pump configured to draw air through a port to create a vacuum". No affirmative passage in the disclosure or in any USER turn recites a sealed region or a bounding function.
findings.fix: Delete numeral 18 and every recitation of the sealed region. In claim 1 restore "a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip;" and "an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body, the electric vacuum pump configured to draw air through a port to create a grip vacuum, the grip vacuum retaining a load on the suction cup;". In claim 4 replace the placing step with "placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece;" and the evacuating step with "drawing air through a port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery, so as to create a grip vacuum;". In draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3 define the term without the region: "The grip vacuum is the vacuum created by the electric vacuum pump 20 and monitored by the pressure sensor 30, expressed as a positive magnitude. The grip vacuum rises as air is removed by the electric vacuum pump 20 and falls as air leaks back. The grip vacuum is lost when air leaks back and the grip vacuum falls." Make the corresponding deletions in ¶7, ¶9, ¶19 and ¶31, in draft/06-summary.md ¶3 and ¶11, and in draft/10-abstract.md ("a suction cup carrying a flexible sealing lip"). Remove the sealed-region bullet and the numeral 18 rows/lists from the FIG. 2 brief.
